analysis.one_liner: Ends a tax deduction that lets publicly traded corporations write off executive bonuses above $1 million.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on April 29, 2015 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law lets publicly traded companies deduct unlimited executive pay beyond $1 million per person, as long as the pay is tied to a performance goal or commission — a carve-out that has turned the $1 million cap into an easily avoided rule. This bill would remove that carve-out, extend the cap to former executives collecting payouts after leaving, and apply it to any corporation required to file reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The effect is that publicly traded companies would pay more in taxes when they hand out multimillion-dollar bonuses, raising revenue for the public treasury.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise help absorb the cost of unlimited executive pay deductions through forgone federal revenue; and the public treasury, which would collect more tax from companies paying large bonuses.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the exemption that lets corporations deduct commission-based and performance-goal compensation above $1 million, the route most large companies used to deduct unlimited bonuses [S2][S3].
Extends the $1 million deduction cap to former officers, directors, and employees, closing the route of departing executives collecting large post-employment payouts [S2][S3].
Applies the cap to any corporation required to register securities or file periodic reports with the SEC, broadening coverage beyond the current narrower definition [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations and their highest-paid executives, who would lose the ability to deduct bonuses and golden-parachute payments above $1 million from their corporate taxes, increasing companies' tax bills.
analysis.who_pays_short: Publicly traded companies and top executives

drawbacks.text: Companies would pay higher taxes on large incentive and retention packages, and business groups generally argue that limiting the deductibility of incentive pay raises corporate costs and could affect how companies structure compensation. This objection is not documented in the provided sources.

The cap is a blunt tool: it applies at $1 million regardless of company size or performance, so it would also cover, for example, high-earning sales staff on commission at smaller SEC-reporting firms rather than only multimillion-dollar executive bonuses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: forgone federal revenue from executive pay deductions would be recovered from companies that pay bonuses far above $1 million. The cost falls on publicly traded companies and their executives, not on ordinary workers, and the bill's own design focuses the burden on the largest compensation packages. The strongest honest objection is that the cap does not distinguish executive pay from other high-dollar compensation, which could complicate pay structures at SEC-reporting firms generally.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing or vote, until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on April 29, 2015 with 23 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is the committee that handles tax legislation [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 49 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
The complete action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action after the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded corporations and their highest-paid executives, who kept the ability to deduct unlimited bonuses above $1 million as a tax write-off for the remainder of the 114th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Publicly traded companies and top executives

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push to close the executive bonus deduction loophole

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from one party

sides.party_line_note: All 50 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsored it; because the bill never reached a vote, there is no roll-call record of where Republicans stood.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their top executives
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated their federal tax deduction for bonuses and golden parachutes above $1 million per person, meaning higher corporate tax bills when they pay multimillion-dollar executive compensation. Its failure left the deduction intact, so companies continue to reduce their taxes with executive pay.
